findings.title: Delete-cache action shown for delegation/team credentials that the handler rejects
findings.body: deleteCacheHandler authorizes solely by `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. Delegation credentials (and team credentials with a null userId) are owned by a different user/admin, so this lookup returns null and the mutation throws "Credential not found or access denied". However, CredentialActionsDropdown only hides the remove-app action for delegation (`canDisconnect = !delegationCredentialId && ...`); it still renders the "Delete cached data" action whenever `hasCache` is truthy, and delegated Google calendars do have a cache row keyed by that credential's DB id, so `cacheUpdatedAt` is set. Result: delegated/team users see "Delete cached data" but every attempt fails with the error toast. Either authorize using the same rule that builds connectedCalendars, or hide the delete action when the credential isn't owned by the session user.

findings.title: Deleting cache does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status
findings.body: deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess only calls `onSuccess?.()` (= props.onChanged). Unlike disconnectMutation, which explicitly invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in onSettled, the cache mutation never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. When the parent does not pass a refetching `onChanged` (it is optional in SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper), the tRPC cache retains the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so after a successful delete the dropdown still shows "Cache Status" and "Delete cached data" until a manual page reload. Invalidate the connectedCalendars query in onSuccess/onSettled as the disconnect path does.

findings.title: No test for deleteCache authorization ceiling
findings.body: deleteCache permanently deletes calendar cache rows and its only safety property is the ownership check. There is no test asserting that a user cannot delete the cache of a credential they do not own (mutation should reject) and can delete their own. Given this is a destructive, authorization-gated mutation, a unit/integration test covering the not-owner rejection and the owner success path should be added before merge.

findings.title: Migration backfills all existing caches with the migration timestamp
findings.body: Adding `updatedAt TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` sets every pre-existing CalendarCache row to the migration run time. getCacheStatusByCredentialIds surfaces this value as "Last updated", so for the existing rows the UI will report the deploy time as the last update for up to the cache TTL (CACHING_TIME = 30 days), which is misleading. Since the real update time can be approximated as `expiresAt - CACHING_TIME`, consider backfilling with that (or leaving the column nullable for legacy rows) instead of NOW().

findings.title: sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only and breaks on GNU/Linux
findings.body: `sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the macOS form of `sed -i`. On GNU sed (typical Linux dev boxes / CI) `-i` treats `''` as the (empty) suffix and then interprets the following expression/arguments incorrectly, so the inline replacement fails and GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is left unchanged (or the command errors). Use a portable approach (e.g. write to a temp file and move it, or detect the OS) so the script works cross-platform.

findings.title: Unnecessary SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update with no reader
findings.body: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now ends with `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`. This issues an extra UPDATE across all SelectedCalendars for the credential on every cache population (i.e. every sync/webhook), only to bump `@updatedAt`, yet nothing reads SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for display — the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt via cacheUpdatedAt. The PR notes this too. It is dead work on a latency-sensitive path; remove it (or add the consumer that justifies it).
